182	 INTRODUCTION
183	On September 16, 2025, the State charged Tyler Robinson with the capital offense of
184	aggravated murder, and other lesser offenses. The State had over ten months to investigate the
185	shooting death of Charlie Kirk and to develop legally sufficient evidence that Mr. Robinson
186	“knowingly created a great risk of death to another other than Charlie Kirk and the defendant,”
187	the sole aggravator alleged in the Information which in theory exposes Mr. Robinson to the
188	potential punishment of death. Utah Code § 76-5-202(2)(a)(iii).
189	The State’s presentation of its evidence as to this alleged circumstance in aggravation at
190	the preliminary hearing in July 2026 wholly fails to carry its burden of proof. The State’s failure
191	cannot in any manner be attributed to any orders by this Court limiting its presentation, nor does
192	it fall within Rule 1102(c)(1) because the State’s presentation in support of this aggravating
193	factor was not based upon hearsay evidence. Nor did this Court exclude any proffered expert
194	testimony. In fact, the Court did not exclude any evidence on this subject, and it did not limit the
195	amount of time available to the State to present its case.
196	Yet, the State has failed to establish probable cause that the shooter “knowingly created a
197	great risk of death to another other than Charlie Kirk” and himself. The State is required, as a
198	matter of law, to show more than a “possibility” that someone else may be killed by defendant’s
199	conduct, rather that there was a “high probability” of that result and that the defendant knew of
200	that high probability. And where the State has overwhelmingly failed to make this showing, it
201	asks this Court to expand Utah’s narrow construction of the “great risk of death” aggravator
202	using decades old cases from another state jurisdiction. Binding constitutional precedent both
203	under Utah law and the United States Constitution demonstrate the State’s failure here and why
204	this Court may not impermissibly broaden the scope of “knowingly created a great risk of death.”
205	The facts and the law require this Court to strike the sole aggravating factor.

 INTRODUCTION
On September 16, 2025, the State charged Tyler Robinson with the capital offense of
aggravated murder, and other lesser offenses. The State had over ten months to investigate the
shooting death of Charlie Kirk and to develop legally sufficient evidence that Mr. Robinson
“knowingly created a great risk of death to another other than Charlie Kirk and the defendant,”
the sole aggravator alleged in the Information which in theory exposes Mr. Robinson to the
potential punishment of death. Utah Code § 76-5-202(2)(a)(iii).
The State’s presentation of its evidence as to this alleged circumstance in aggravation at
the preliminary hearing in July 2026 wholly fails to carry its burden of proof. The State’s failure
cannot in any manner be attributed to any orders by this Court limiting its presentation, nor does
it fall within Rule 1102(c)(1) because the State’s presentation in support of this aggravating
factor was not based upon hearsay evidence. Nor did this Court exclude any proffered expert
testimony. In fact, the Court did not exclude any evidence on this subject, and it did not limit the
amount of time available to the State to present its case.
Yet, the State has failed to establish probable cause that the shooter “knowingly created a
great risk of death to another other than Charlie Kirk” and himself. The State is required, as a
matter of law, to show more than a “possibility” that someone else may be killed by defendant’s
conduct, rather that there was a “high probability” of that result and that the defendant knew of
that high probability. And where the State has overwhelmingly failed to make this showing, it
asks this Court to expand Utah’s narrow construction of the “great risk of death” aggravator
using decades old cases from another state jurisdiction. Binding constitutional precedent both
under Utah law and the United States Constitution demonstrate the State’s failure here and why
this Court may not impermissibly broaden the scope of “knowingly created a great risk of death.”
The facts and the law require this Court to strike the sole aggravating factor.

a. The United States Constitution and the Utah Constitution Both Require Courts to
Construe Alleged Aggravators Narrowly.
“The Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments to the United States Constitution do not permit
imposition of the death penalty in an arbitrary or capricious manner.” State v. Wood, 648 P.2d
71, 77 (Utah 1982). “The objective of the law is to require that the discretion of a sentencing
body in a capital case be carefully channeled by standards designed and applied to insure that
there is a reasonable distinction between those murder cases in which the death penalty is

holdings to this effect).
In order to bring meaning to this long-standing principle, the United States Supreme
Court has explained that the Constitution requires courts to narrowly construe aggravating
factors in order to avoid “overly broad interpretation[s]” that violate the Eighth and Fourteenth
Amendments. See, e.g., Gregg v. Georgia, 428 U.S. 153, 202 (1976).
The United States Supreme Court has twice examined the “KGRD” aggravator at issue
here. In Gregg, the Court upheld the inclusion of KGRD as a statutory aggravating circumstance:
While such a phrase might be susceptible of an overly broad interpretation, the
Supreme Court of Georgia has not so construed it. The only case in which the
court upheld a conviction in reliance on this aggravating circumstance involved a
man who stood up in a church and fired a gun indiscriminately into the audience.
See Chenault v. State, [215 S.E.2d 223 (Ga. 1975)]. On the other hand, the court
expressly reversed a finding of great risk when the victim was simply kidnaped in
a parking lot. See Jarrell v. State, [216 S.E.2d 258, 269 (Ga. 1975)].
428 U.S. at 202-03. The same year, in Proffitt v. Florida, 428 U.S. 242, 255 (1976), the Court
upheld the use of KGRD as an aggravator based upon the Florida Supreme Court’s decision in
Alvord v. State, 322 So. 2d 553 (1975) which also construed KGRD narrowly. In Alvord, KGRD
was “obvious[ ]” because the defendant “murdered two of the victims in order to avoid a
surviving witness to the (first) murder.” Proffitt, 428 U.S. at 256. 2
In each of these cases, the Court considered whether the statutory aggravating
circumstance was too vague and overbroad to pass Eighth and Fourteenth Amendment muster
and in each, the Court upheld the aggravator because the States’ highest courts had narrowly
construed them.
The principle that the death penalty may not be “wantonly and freakishly imposed”
“requires a state to channel the sentencer’s discretion by ‘clear and objective standards’ that
provide ‘specific and detailed guidance[.]” Lewis v. Jeffers, 497 U.S. 764, 774 (1990) (citation

b. Utah Supreme Court Decisions Narrowly Construing the KGRD Aggravator Require
This Court to Strike It Here.
Over the course of the past 50 years, the Utah Supreme Court has had at least three
opportunities to carefully consider the KGRD aggravator. In doing so, it has identified a
minimum set of factual circumstances which must be present in order for the aggravator to be
applied in a constitutionally valid manner. Mr. Robinson addresses here the three decisions by
this State’s highest court which, when applied to the facts presented here, compel this Court to
strike the alleged aggravator because those constitutionally required factors are not present.
Those Utah Supreme Court cases are its decisions in State v. Sosa-Hurtado, 2019 UT 65,
455 P.3d 63 (“Sosa-Hurtado II”), and two long-standing decisions in State v. Johnson, 740 P.2d
1264, 1265-66 (Utah 1987) and State v. Pierre, 572 P.2d 1338, 1342 (Utah 1977). They are
addressed below in chronological order so that this Court can see how the doctrine which this
Court must apply in this case has evolved to require, as a factual matter, that where one or more
firearm is used in a homicide, the defendant actually discharges multiple rounds, hitting and/or
killing individual(s) other than the murder victim in series of events. These actions are the
“concatenating series of events” which the Utah Supreme Court first referred to in its 1997
decision in State v. Pierre and then reaffirmed in its decision in Sosa-Hurtado II that may lead
the Court to conclude that the conduct alleged created a “high probability” that someone other
than the victim and defendant would be killed.
One year after the United States Supreme Court decisions in Gregg and Proffitt, the Utah
Supreme Court considered the application of KGRD in State v. Pierre, 572 P.2d at 1342. In
Pierre, the defendant was convicted of three counts of capital murder. Pierre and two
codefendants tied up five individuals in a business establishment and forced them to drink liquid

d. This Court Must Reject the State’s Asserted Theories as to How It Has Established
Facts Supporting the KGRD Aggravator Because It Has Failed to Establish the Facts
That Are Constitutionally Required.
The State offers two interrelated theories of KGRD that fail to conform to the criteria
established by the Utah Supreme Court, criteria which if not met render application of the KGRD
aggravator violative of U.S. Const. amend. VIII, XIV and Utah Const. art. I, § 9. Each is
deconstructed here.
First, the State has propounded a “line of sight” theory which is based upon out-of-state
authority that has never been adopted in Utah. It is primarily based upon the decisions of courts
in Pennsylvania before that state enacted a moratorium. 10 Moreover, the State’s reliance on this

10

For over a decade, Pennsylvania has had a moratorium on the death penalty.

15

 authority fails to support the application of a “line of sight” formulation to the facts it presented
at the preliminary hearing. The State’s “line of sight” theory as applied to the “questioner” to the
East and below Mr. Kirk fails based upon the facts the State presented to this Court and no
further reasonable inferences based upon those facts can support that basis for the aggravator.
The second theory is an “everyone near” argument, which relies upon only one of the
three factors identified in Sosa-Hurtado II, and ignores the other two factors which are not
present here. Moreover, the State asks the Court to speculate about the shooter’s knowledge.
Even assuming that one can infer a knowledge of some risk to the shooter, the State has failed to
show that the actual conduct created a “high probability” that someone other than Mr. Kirk
would be killed and, thus, this theory fails as a matter of law. Where there were people in some
proximity to a discharge of a single projectile from a precision firearm with a high-powered
scope which the evidence establishes hit its intended target, the single factor of proximity fails to
permit an inference of a subjective knowledge of the shooter of a high probability of risk of
death to others. Where no other person was injured in a manner creating a great risk of death, and
no other shots were fired, the allegation of a KGRD aggravator cannot be sustained.
i. Line of Sight.
The State broadly argues that certain individuals were in the shooter’s “line of fire.”
There are two fatal flaws in the State’s argument—one is factual, and the other is legal.
Factually, the “line of fire” assertion as to the questioner defies logic. The evidence
established that there was one shooter on the roof of the Losee Center. Mr. Kirk was seated
under a pop-up tent in the center of a courtyard to the southwest of where the shooter was
positioned on the roof. See PH1:27 (Losee directly east of amphitheater). The single shot fired
travelled from east to west at a downward slope into the bottom of the “bowl” where the tent was
located. See StEx 8, at 00:35 (showing crowd at increasing elevation to the East of the pop-up
tent); see also StEx 3. State’s Exhibit 7 shows the vantage behind the questioner prior to and at
12:23:28 PM. The questioner is in front of Mr. Kirk—to the East. If the questioner had been in
the “line of fire” from a bullet moving towards Mr. Kirk, the questioner would have been struck
16

 by the bullet as it travelled. In fact, the State’s evidence shows exactly why the questioner was
not in the line of fire—the single bullet came from above. The video evidence shows that Mr.
Kirk was seated on an elevated platform and separated from the questioner by a security barrier,
a grassy area, and then tables that surrounded Mr. Kirk on three sides. StEx 8, at 00:35. The
bullet traveled at a downward angle and hit Mr. Kirk in the left side of his neck. See PH4:91-92;
StEx 11. Where Mr. Kirk’s head/neck area was elevated and an unidentified distance away from
the questioner (certainly more than a “few feet” away 11), the only evidence presented supports
that the bullet travelled above, not through, the crowd.

917	expands Utah’s KGRD aggravator beyond its constitutionally narrow application, as explained in
918	Sosa-Hurtado II, Johnson, and Pierre. Utah law requires this Court to look at more than mere
919	presence and to determine there is a “high probability,” not a “mere possibility” that another
920	would be killed by the shooter’s conduct and that the shooter knew of that high probability.
921	e. A Plenary of Jurisdictions Support Utah’s Narrow Construction of KGRD.
922	Many other jurisdictions have interpreted KGRD as the Utah Supreme Court has—a
923	multifactor analysis that examines the course of conduct of the defendant and actions toward the
924	“another” in determining both the defendant’s knowledge and the probability of risk.
925	For example, Oklahoma has determined that evidence is sufficient to support KGRD
926	where “the defendant created a great risk of death in close proximity in terms of time, location,
927	24
928	
929	 and intent to the killing, or threatened the life of another and had the apparent ability and means
930	of taking that person’s life.” Lockett v. Trammel, 711 F.3d 1218, 1243 (10th Cir. 2013) (internal
931	citations omitted) (cleaned up). In the rare instances where the person at risk was not actually
932	injured, “the defendants in those cases seriously considered killing people other than the actual
933	victims.” Valdez v. State, 900 P.2d 363, 383 & n.97 (Okla. Crim. App. 1995).
934	In the Oklahoma case of Littlejohn v. State, 989 P.2d 901 (Okla. Crim. App. 1998), the
935	court considered the sufficiency of the evidence supporting KGRD. The court found the evidence
936	was insufficient to support KGRD aggravating factor where the prosecution presented no
937	evidence that defendant “considered injuring anyone other than the actual victim.” Id. at 912.
938	Although defendant pointed a gun at a clerk when he asked for the store’s money, this act was
939	driven by defendant’s intent to rob. Id. Additionally, only a single shot was fired and it hit its
940	intended victim, rather than endangering anyone else present in the store. Id. As summarized:
941	This is not a case where the defendant shot wildly into a store or a crowd. Only
942	one shot was fired. This shot hit its intended victim. This single shot did not
943	endanger anyone else present in the store. Consequently, under the specific
944	circumstances of this case, we find the evidence was insufficient to prove
945	Littlejohn knowingly created a great risk of death to more than one person.
946	Id. See also Brecheen v. Reynolds, 41 F.3d 1343, 1361 (10th Cir. 1994) (rejecting Eighth
947	Amendment vagueness challenge to KGRD because reviewing Oklahoma case law, “Oklahoma
948	courts provided consistent guidance to the jury so as to limit its discretion”).
949	The Wyoming Supreme Court upheld KGRD in Engberg v. State, 668 P.2d 541 (Wyo.
950	1984), concluding: “In shooting errantly at persons in parked vehicles in the lot, Engberg
951	manifested an utter disregard for lives of innocent persons. This evidence demonstrated beyond a
952	reasonable doubt that Engberg knowingly created a great risk of death to two or more persons.”
953	Id. at 557 (emphasis added). Later, Olsen v. State, 2003 WY 46, 67 P.3d 536, addressed another
954	“bystander” case. The Olsen Court noted the State failed to produce evidence or suggest “that
955	there were other bystanders involved who were threatened with grave harm as Olsen shot his
956	intended victims.” Id. ¶ 121. Thus, “[s]trictly construing the Wyoming statute” the Olsen Court
957	found “the use of the terms ‘risk’ and ‘persons’ was given its proper application in Engberg’s
958	25
959	
960	 factual situation of placing bystanders in a parking lot at great risk of death by errant shooting.”
961	Id. ¶ 123.
962	In the Alabama case of White v. State, 587 So. 2d 1218, 1232 (Ala. Crim. App. 1990), the
963	appellate court upheld the finding of KGRD where, “the defendant indiscriminately fired a
964	shotgun into an occupied dwelling containing not only the victim but two other people” and “the
965	defendant fired the pistol out in the front yard in a residential neighborhood where many other
966	people were present.” The Court found “the defendant’s conduct in the indiscriminate firing of
967	these weapons did, in fact, create a great risk of death to many other people.” Id.
968	Finally, there is also an almost identical federal statutory aggravator. See 18 U.S.C. §

974	such force as to create a risk to persons who were not physically affected by the explosion.”

976	bombing case, the district court sanctioned the inclusion of KGRD as an aggravator noting
977	KGRD “relates to Defendants’ mental state with respect to persons who were not the intended
978	victims of the bombings.” The Bin Laden Court noted, there may be “a qualitative difference
979	between a defendant who carefully targets an intended victim or victims without endangering
980	others, and one who acts with indifference to ‘additional persons.’” Id. n.15.

1074	III.
1075	
1076	Count Seven Must Be Stricken Because the Evidence Does Not Establish That Mr.
1077	Robinson Had Knowledge That a Child Under the Age of 14 Was Present and
1078	Would See or Hear the Commission of the Charged Homicide.
1079	The Information charges Mr. Robinson, in Count Seven, with the substantive offense of
1080	
1081	knowingly exposing a child under the age of 14 to the charged homicide, in violation of Utah
1082	Code § 76-3-203-10(2).
1083	This section of Utah law requires that the State prove that a violent offense occurred “in
1084	the physical presence of a child younger than 14 years old” with the defendant “having
1085	knowledge that the child is present and may see or hear the commission of a violent criminal
1086	offense.” Utah Code § 76-3-203-10(2).
1087	The State has failed to present sufficient evidence to establish probable cause that Mr.
1088	Robinson did in fact have the requisite knowledge. While the State presented a video which
1089	shows two children, in fact, present at the TPUSA rally at UVU on September 10, 2025, the
1090	State presented no evidence that the shooter was aware of this child’s presence, nor that he was
1091	aware of the presence of any other child under the age of 14. See StEx 6.
1092	Without any evidentiary support, the State invites this Court to speculate that Mr.
1093	Robinson, from approximately 400 feet away and during a 35-44 second period, came to be
1094	aware of the presence of children under the age of 14, relying upon Mr. Robinson’s alleged
1095	walking tour of the campus several hours before the TPUSA rally began. There was no evidence
1096	that Mr. Robinson was anywhere near the crowd that formed prior to the rally, or that he
1097	observed children or families with children making their way to the space where the rally
1098	occurred. Indeed, the path Mr. Robinson travelled as visible in State’s Exhibits 12.1 and 12.4
1099	suggests Mr. Robinson did not even pass anyone that could be identified as under 14 years old.
1100	
1101	29
1102	
1103	 The reasonable inferences might differ if the location of the incident were not a college
1104	campus. If a defendant were to engage in crimes of violence at an obviously occupied elementary
1105	school or a day care facility, it might be reasonable to infer the knowledge required under Count
1106	Seven. With the evidence as it is, this is not a reasonable inference.
1107	a. The “Violent Offense Committed in the Presence of a Child” Aggravating Factor
1108	Must Be Stricken for the Same Reason—There Is No Evidence That Mr. Robinson
1109	Had the Requisite Knowledge.
1110	Separate and apart from Count Seven, the State has alleged the identical aggravating
1111	factor in connection with Counts One and Two, pursuant to Utah Code section 76-3-203.9. The
1112	analysis is no different. There is no evidence that Mr. Robinson had the requisite knowledge and
1113	the State improperly invites the Court to speculate. See Murphy, 2026 UT App 38, ¶ 10 (“An
1114	inference is a conclusion reached by considering other facts and deducing a logical consequence
1115	from them,” and speculation entails “the act or practice of theorizing about matters over which
1116	there is no certain knowledge at hand.” (citation omitted)). Id.
1117	b. The State’s Backup Position, That Sentencing Enhancements Are Not Subject to
1118	Proof at a Preliminary Hearing, Is Inconsistent with Well-Established Constitutional
1119	Law.
1120	The State asserts that the enhancements alleged in the Information are not subject to this
1121	Court’s review in a preliminary hearing. The State is incorrect about this important matter and
1122	relies on an invalidated distinction between “elements” and “sentencing factors”. While the Utah
1123	Supreme Court did so hold in cases in the 1970s and 1980s, in the year 2000 the United States
1124	Supreme Court squarely held that any fact which increases the potential punishment in a case,
1125	other than criminal history facts, are elements of the offense which must be proven to a jury
1126	beyond a reasonable doubt. Apprendi v. New Jersey 530 U.S. 466 (1980). In fact, the Court
1127	wrote, “It is unconstitutional for a legislature to remove from the jury the assessment of facts that
1128	increase the prescribed range of penalties to which a criminal defendant is exposed. It is equally
1129	clear that such facts must be established by proof beyond a reasonable doubt.” Id. at 490.
1130	Here, the State has charged Mr. Robinson, in an Information subject to a probable cause
1131	determination, with two separate sentencing enhancements, each of which carries the possibility
1132	30
1133	
1134	 of increasing Mr. Robinson’s punishment. Utah Code § 76-3-203.9 requires the sentencing court
1135	or the Board of Pardons and Parole to consider whether “the knowing presence of a child”
1136	enhancement has been proven in the course of exercising their authority over sentencing and
1137	release decisions. Utah Code § 6-3-203.14 is a “victim targeting enhancement” which makes
1138	“one classification higher” the offense for which the defendant was convicted. Therefore, it too is
1139	subject to Apprendi.
1140	Where the State has elected not to proceed by way of grand jury but instead elects to
1141	present the evidence in support of its Information to a magistrate, the defendant’s constitutional
1142	right not to be tried on any of the charged offenses absent an initial finding of probable cause
1143	extends to enhancements that increase the potential punishment. This is a logical consequence of
1144	Apprendi, which eliminated, with exceptions not applicable here, the distinction between
1145	elements of an offense and sentencing factors which increase the maximum punishment.
1146	The State must prove each of the enhancements to this Court, sitting as a Magistrate, by
1147	probable cause. As to the “violent offense committed in the presence of a child” Mr. Robinson
1148	has explained above why the State has failed to meet its burden of proof. Mr. Robinson now
1149	turns to the second enhancement alleged in the Information, the allegation that Mr. Robinson
1150	selected Mr. Kirk based upon Mr. Robinson’s views of Mr. Kirk’s political expression.

1153	The State Has Failed to Produce Reliable Evidence That the “Victim Targeting
1154	Enhancement” Applies Here.

1156	
1157	focused on the defendant’s perception concerning a “personal attribute” of the victim. The single
1158	“personal attribute” alleged in the Information is Mr. Kirk’s “political expression” (§ 76-3203(14)(1)(k)) without any further specificity in the charging document. In support of this
1159	enhancement, the State proffers two disconnected sets of facts which fail to establish probable
1160	cause.
1161	One set is Exhibit 5.1, a Rule 1102 witness statement of David Englehardt, a pastor.
1162	Pastor Englehardt’s statement contains no information concerning Mr. Robinson’s state of mind
1163	31
1164	
1165	 as to Mr. Kirk’s political expressions. While it purports to present this Court with information as
1166	to what Charlie Kirk believed “as all theologically-orthodox-Christians believe” about gender
1167	identity and sexuality, it does not identity any specific statements made by Mr. Kirk on these
1168	topics prior to September 10, 2025. It also identifies subject matters that Mr. Kirk would debate
1169	and discuss at various events, but it does not identify a specific political expression of Mr. Kirk
1170	on such topics, let alone statements of Mr. Kirk that were both known to and motivated Mr.
1171	Robinson.
1172	Therefore, Mr. Englehardt’s written sermon as to what “all theologically-orthodoxChristians” including Mr. Kirk “believe” does not establish that Mr. Robinson “intentionally”
1173	selected “the victim of the criminal offense because of the defendant’s belief or perception
1174	regarding the victim’s personal attribute or a personal attribute of another individual or group of
1175	individuals with whom the victim has a relationship.”
1176	The only other “fact” is Mr. Robinson’s statement to Mr. Twiggs, “I had enough of his
1177	hatred.” StEx 16.1. Mr. Robinson does not tell Mr. Twiggs in this text exchange, nor was there,
1178	according to Mr. Twiggs, any prior communication between them concerning Mr. Kirk, nor that
1179	Mr. Robinson targeted Mr. Kirk because of his religious beliefs or his political beliefs or any
1180	other category of beliefs. He refers to “hatred” and nothing more.
1181	Ironically, it is the State that argues that because Mr. Robinson and Mr. Twiggs are two
1182	men who love each other and/or, it speculates, because Mr. Twiggs (and not Mr. Robinson) was
1183	at least intermittently identifying as a female to his close friends, it is Mr. Kirk’s views on these
1184	topics which are the “hatred” Mr. Robinson was referring to.
1185	These circumstances are not sufficient to establish, even by probable cause which if any
1186	political expression of Mr. Kirk motivated Mr. Robinson to select Mr. Kirk for an act of
1187	violence. There is no evidence of specific political expressions of Mr. Kirk which, if any, Mr.
1188	Robinson may have been aware of or focused on. There are no writings attributed to Mr.
1189	Robinson on this topic. There are no other statements by Mr. Robinson to third parties which
1190	address Mr. Kirk or his political viewpoints and Mr. Robinson’s perception of them. After
1191	32
1192	
1193	 searching his residence, his parents’ residence, his computers, his telephone, Mr. Twiggs’
1194	telephone, and hundreds of law enforcement interviews, there is nothing to base this sentencing
1195	enhancement upon other than that single criticism of Mr. Kirk’s “hatred”.
1196	In the face of the absence of evidence, the State focuses on Mr. Robinson’s sexuality and
1197	Mr. Twiggs’ gender identity, if only because those are two topics on which Mr. Kirk was, in fact,
1198	widely viewed as expressing hatred and intolerance. However, that is not an evidentiary
1199	substitute for proof that Mr. Robinson targeted Mr. Kirk because of those expressions. It is the
1200	State’s speculation that he did so.
1201	The victim targeting enhancement must be stricken.
1202	CONCLUSION
1203	In relying largely on hearsay deemed reliable by rule, the State has failed to prove
1204	probable cause by reliable evidence that satisfies each element of each of the charged evidence.
1205	For this reason alone, this Court must decline bindover. In addition, the State has not provided
1206	this Court with sufficient evidence, as a matter of law, to satisfy the sole alleged aggravator in
1207	the Information. Under controlling constitutional law and Utah Supreme Court interpretation, the
1208	Court cannot find based on the State’s evidence that the circumstances presented a great risk of
1209	death to another other than Charlie Kirk and himself, and that the shooter knew of this “high
1210	probability” of death of another. Finally, the Court should decline to bindover on the State’s
1211	alleged aggravators and Counts 6 and 7 where the State requires this Court to speculate in the
1212	absence of evidence to establish essential elements.

Court considered the application of Pennsylvania’s “grave risk” aggravator to a case in which
Watson fired three shots into an occupied car, striking an individual twice. Watson then shot the
lock off the door of a home, pulled his ex-girlfriend from the closet where she was hiding with
her two children, and shot her twice. Id. He then reloaded, left the room, returned, and then shot
her again and then shot himself. Id. One of the shots lodged in the door frame around the closet
where the children were hiding but did not hit them. Id. Under these facts, the Pennsylvania court
affirmed a jury’s finding as to the KGRD aggravating factor because the children in the closet
were endangered by his conduct. Id.
In Silvia v. State, 60 So. 3d 959, 971-73 (Fla. 2011), the defendant argued that there “was
not competent, substantial evidence” to support KGRD because the gunfire was intended only
for one person. Id. at 971. The Florida Supreme Court disagreed because Silvia engaged in

We therefore conclude there was competent, substantial evidence that
Silvia’s actions created a great risk of death to many persons. He approached the

Id.
In Commonwealth v. Reid, 626 A.2d 118, 123 (Pa. 1993), the Pennsylvania Supreme
Court found sufficient evidence to uphold the “grave risk” aggravating circumstance. Reid had
fired multiple gunshots at fleeing children after chasing them in his vehicle. Id. at 119. One of
the shots hit a young man in the back, killing him. Id. Less than a week later, Reid killed another
individual with the same weapon. Id. The Court noted that “twelve to fourteen others were in the
line of fire” when Reid “chased the boys while driving his car” and “gunfire flashed from the
windows of Reid’s car” killing the first victim. Id. n.3.
In Commonwealth v. Buck, 709 A.2d 892 (Pa. 1998), the court considered whether the
Commonwealth’s notice to the defendant of the aggravating circumstance was sufficient and if
the Commonwealth abused its discretion in proceeding on three aggravators, one of them “grave
risk.” Id. at 897-98. In finding the Commonwealth did not abuse its discretion in alleging “grave
risk,” the Buck Court found that evidence raised a factual question for the jury because, while
only one individual was shot and killed, the potentially endangered person stood behind the
decedent in a bathroom and, importantly, because the endangered person wrestled with the
defendant over the gun after the shot was fired. Id.
In State v. Wood, 881 P.2d 1158 (Ariz. 1994), Wood challenged the application of KGRD
in a double-murder case where he did not shoot any persons other than the victims and there
were no bystanders in the line of fire. Id. at 69. The court found that although the defendant’s
18

 argument had merit, the interpretation of KGRD proposed was too narrow “under the unusual
facts” of the case. Id. The Wood Court found “no single factor is dispositive” of KGRD and the
inquiry turns on “whether, during the court of the killing, the defendant knowingly engaged in
conduct that created a real and substantial likelihood that a specific person might suffer fatal
injury.” Id. Thus, the several factors “in combination” supported KGRD. Id. (emphasis in
original). There was the presence of others, the defendant turned to another and it appeared as if
he was going to shoot a third individual, another employee fought defendant over the gun, and
there was evidence the defendant “knowingly prepared the gun to fire when he assumed a
shooting stance toward one employee and when he grappled with another.” Id.
None of these cases support the State’s position here. Each involves conduct directed at
the endangered person, consistent with the Utah Supreme Court’s endorsement of the three “zone
of danger” factors in Sosa-Hurtado II. In determining if KGRD applies, as a matter of law, this
Court must consider if any conduct constituting a great risk of death was directed at any
individuals other than the victim. Here, there is none.
Utah has never adopted an interpretation of KGRD that would permit its application
where the firing of a single shot at an intended victim that hit only the intended victim, merely
because other people were in the vicinity. Nor does the State’s reliance on out of state authorities
in which personas other than the decedent are targeted and/or injured support this proposition. As
a matter of law, the Court cannot bind Mr. Robinson over on this theory of the KGRD aggravator
based on the facts presented by the State.
ii. The State’s “Anyone Near” Argument Similarly Fails Both Factually and as a
Matter of Law.
The State’s second argument in support of the KGRD aggravator is that the shooter
knowingly “created a great risk of death to everyone near Mr. Kirk” when a single shot was fired.
StBr:14. The State’s argument here also fails because it requires the Court to speculate in the
absence of evidence that would otherwise permit reasonable inferences. Moreover, the State’s
argument fails again, as a matter of law, because the conduct here fails to satisfy any of the three
19

 factors the Utah Supreme Court has held must be present in order for the KGRD aggravator to be
pursued in a manner which does not violate a defendant’s constitutional rights under the Eighth
and Fourteenth Amendments.
1. Knowledge.
The State asks this Court to make a finding that the shooter knowingly created a “high
probability of a grave risk of death” based upon speculation that is not supported by the

2. Presence Alone Is Insufficient as a Matter of Law to Show KGRD.
Even assuming arguendo that the shooter had knowledge that there were other
individuals near Mr. Kirk, this fact alone does not satisfy that there was great risk of death to
another. The State relies on cases from Pennsylvania for the assertion that “a zone of danger
encompasses everyone near a shooting victim.” StBr:16-17. As noted above, Utah has never
adopted a formulation of KGRD under which a single gunshot fired at a specifically identified
target who was near others is sufficient to establish KGRD. Moreover, the cases cited by the
State from Pennsylvania, again, do not support its position, as explained below.
In Commonwealth v. Rios, 684 A.2d 1025 (Pa. 1996), three assailants entered a home to
commit a robbery. The residence was occupied by four individuals. Two of the individuals were
beaten and multiple firearms were involved. All four of the victims were forced to lay down
either on a bed or on the floor in a single bedroom, and one of them was shot and killed. Id. at
1028. The court found that the facts presented at trial supported the KGRD finding because the
fatal bullet was fired “while the victim lay on the floor of an enclosed bedroom” with one
individual “on the floor close to the victim” and the others on the bed nearby. Id. at 1037.
In Commonwealth v. Ly, 599 A.2d 613, 622 (Pa. 1991), the court upheld the finding of
“grave risk” when three assailants with multiple firearms shot one individual in the head inside
the kitchen of a restaurant while the murder victim’s sister was “standing directly next to” her.
In Commonwealth v. Smith, 540 A.2d 246, 248 (Pa. 1988), the Commonwealth presented
“medical and forensic evidence” to demonstrate “grave risk of death to another person[.]” The
evidence demonstrated that four shots were fired by the defendant. Id. The first shot fired hit the
victim, who fell but then tried to get up. Id. Thereafter, the defendant fired three more shots at
the victim—three of the rounds lodged in the victim while a fourth passed through. One of the
bullets fired at the victim ricocheted off of a solid surface before hitting the victim. Id. at 248.
23

260. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court affirmed the finding by the jury on these facts. Id.
In Commonwealth v. Wright, 961 A.2d 119, 146 (Pa. 2008), the evidence supporting
“grave risk” was that Wright “broke into a small bedroom while swinging his loaded gun in all
directions” then put his gun to the victim’s wife’s head. Once finding the victim, Wright “fired
five shots at him, three of which went through him and one of which was never located.” Id. The
victim was “only a few feet from the bed on which the child was lying, and shell casings were
found all over the bedroom.” Id. The Pennsylvania court determined that under these
circumstances, it was proper to leave “the grave risk of danger determination to the jury.” Id.
The significant factual differences between these cases and the case before this Court are
plain. The bullet that struck and killed Mr. Kirk was not fired in an enclosed bedroom or space
but rather, an open-air arena with what the State’s witnesses termed, “a clear line of sight.” There
were no threats to others in the course of conduct. There was no one “directly” next to Mr. Kirk
when he was shot, and there was no one under the tent on the side that Mr. Kirk was struck or
behind him in the breezeway. Multiple shots were not fired. There were no ricocheting bullets.
These cases, from a state with a moratorium on its own death penalty, are not Utah law
and do not support the State’s call for this Court to adopt out of state authority that vastly
expands Utah’s KGRD aggravator beyond its constitutionally narrow application, as explained in
Sosa-Hurtado II, Johnson, and Pierre. Utah law requires this Court to look at more than mere
presence and to determine there is a “high probability,” not a “mere possibility” that another
would be killed by the shooter’s conduct and that the shooter knew of that high probability.
e. A Plenary of Jurisdictions Support Utah’s Narrow Construction of KGRD.
Many other jurisdictions have interpreted KGRD as the Utah Supreme Court has—a
multifactor analysis that examines the course of conduct of the defendant and actions toward the
“another” in determining both the defendant’s knowledge and the probability of risk.
For example, Oklahoma has determined that evidence is sufficient to support KGRD
where “the defendant created a great risk of death in close proximity in terms of time, location,
24

 and intent to the killing, or threatened the life of another and had the apparent ability and means
of taking that person’s life.” Lockett v. Trammel, 711 F.3d 1218, 1243 (10th Cir. 2013) (internal
citations omitted) (cleaned up). In the rare instances where the person at risk was not actually
injured, “the defendants in those cases seriously considered killing people other than the actual
victims.” Valdez v. State, 900 P.2d 363, 383 & n.97 (Okla. Crim. App. 1995).
In the Oklahoma case of Littlejohn v. State, 989 P.2d 901 (Okla. Crim. App. 1998), the
court considered the sufficiency of the evidence supporting KGRD. The court found the evidence
was insufficient to support KGRD aggravating factor where the prosecution presented no
evidence that defendant “considered injuring anyone other than the actual victim.” Id. at 912.
Although defendant pointed a gun at a clerk when he asked for the store’s money, this act was
driven by defendant’s intent to rob. Id. Additionally, only a single shot was fired and it hit its
intended victim, rather than endangering anyone else present in the store. Id. As summarized:
This is not a case where the defendant shot wildly into a store or a crowd. Only
one shot was fired. This shot hit its intended victim. This single shot did not
endanger anyone else present in the store. Consequently, under the specific
circumstances of this case, we find the evidence was insufficient to prove
Littlejohn knowingly created a great risk of death to more than one person.
Id. See also Brecheen v. Reynolds, 41 F.3d 1343, 1361 (10th Cir. 1994) (rejecting Eighth
Amendment vagueness challenge to KGRD because reviewing Oklahoma case law, “Oklahoma
courts provided consistent guidance to the jury so as to limit its discretion”).
The Wyoming Supreme Court upheld KGRD in Engberg v. State, 668 P.2d 541 (Wyo.
1984), concluding: “In shooting errantly at persons in parked vehicles in the lot, Engberg
manifested an utter disregard for lives of innocent persons. This evidence demonstrated beyond a
reasonable doubt that Engberg knowingly created a great risk of death to two or more persons.”
Id. at 557 (emphasis added). Later, Olsen v. State, 2003 WY 46, 67 P.3d 536, addressed another
“bystander” case. The Olsen Court noted the State failed to produce evidence or suggest “that
there were other bystanders involved who were threatened with grave harm as Olsen shot his
intended victims.” Id. ¶ 121. Thus, “[s]trictly construing the Wyoming statute” the Olsen Court
found “the use of the terms ‘risk’ and ‘persons’ was given its proper application in Engberg’s
25

Id. ¶ 123.
In the Alabama case of White v. State, 587 So. 2d 1218, 1232 (Ala. Crim. App. 1990), the
appellate court upheld the finding of KGRD where, “the defendant indiscriminately fired a
shotgun into an occupied dwelling containing not only the victim but two other people” and “the
defendant fired the pistol out in the front yard in a residential neighborhood where many other
people were present.” The Court found “the defendant’s conduct in the indiscriminate firing of
these weapons did, in fact, create a great risk of death to many other people.” Id.
Finally, there is also an almost identical federal statutory aggravator. See 18 U.S.C. §
3592(c)(5) (“defendant, in the commission of the offense, or in escaping apprehension for the
violation of the offense, knowingly created a grave risk of death to 1 or more persons in addition
to the victim of the offense.”). In United States v. McVeigh, 944 F. Supp. 1478, 1490 (D. Colo.
1996), the Oklahoma City bombing case, the district court found the inclusion of KGRD in the

Similarly, in United States v. Bin Laden, 126 F. Supp. 2d 290, 300 (S.D.N.Y. 2001), another

others, and one who acts with indifference to ‘additional persons.’” Id. n.15.

b. The State’s Backup Position, That Sentencing Enhancements Are Not Subject to

The State asserts that the enhancements alleged in the Information are not subject to this
Court’s review in a preliminary hearing. The State is incorrect about this important matter and
relies on an invalidated distinction between “elements” and “sentencing factors”. While the Utah
Supreme Court did so hold in cases in the 1970s and 1980s, in the year 2000 the United States
Supreme Court squarely held that any fact which increases the potential punishment in a case,
other than criminal history facts, are elements of the offense which must be proven to a jury
beyond a reasonable doubt. Apprendi v. New Jersey 530 U.S. 466 (1980). In fact, the Court
wrote, “It is unconstitutional for a legislature to remove from the jury the assessment of facts that
increase the prescribed range of penalties to which a criminal defendant is exposed. It is equally
clear that such facts must be established by proof beyond a reasonable doubt.” Id. at 490.
Here, the State has charged Mr. Robinson, in an Information subject to a probable cause
determination, with two separate sentencing enhancements, each of which carries the possibility
30

 of increasing Mr. Robinson’s punishment. Utah Code § 76-3-203.9 requires the sentencing court
or the Board of Pardons and Parole to consider whether “the knowing presence of a child”
enhancement has been proven in the course of exercising their authority over sentencing and
release decisions. Utah Code § 6-3-203.14 is a “victim targeting enhancement” which makes
“one classification higher” the offense for which the defendant was convicted. Therefore, it too is
subject to Apprendi.
Where the State has elected not to proceed by way of grand jury but instead elects to
present the evidence in support of its Information to a magistrate, the defendant’s constitutional
right not to be tried on any of the charged offenses absent an initial finding of probable cause
extends to enhancements that increase the potential punishment. This is a logical consequence of
Apprendi, which eliminated, with exceptions not applicable here, the distinction between
elements of an offense and sentencing factors which increase the maximum punishment.
The State must prove each of the enhancements to this Court, sitting as a Magistrate, by
probable cause. As to the “violent offense committed in the presence of a child” Mr. Robinson
has explained above why the State has failed to meet its burden of proof. Mr. Robinson now
turns to the second enhancement alleged in the Information, the allegation that Mr. Robinson
selected Mr. Kirk based upon Mr. Robinson’s views of Mr. Kirk’s political expression.

CONCLUSION
In relying largely on hearsay deemed reliable by rule, the State has failed to prove
probable cause by reliable evidence that satisfies each element of each of the charged evidence.
For this reason alone, this Court must decline bindover. In addition, the State has not provided
this Court with sufficient evidence, as a matter of law, to satisfy the sole alleged aggravator in
the Information. Under controlling constitutional law and Utah Supreme Court interpretation, the
Court cannot find based on the State’s evidence that the circumstances presented a great risk of
death to another other than Charlie Kirk and himself, and that the shooter knew of this “high
probability” of death of another. Finally, the Court should decline to bindover on the State’s
alleged aggravators and Counts 6 and 7 where the State requires this Court to speculate in the
absence of evidence to establish essential elements.

- **M-01** (caption, pp. i/cover): Four signing counsel: Kathryn N. Nester (Nester Lewis PLLC, SLC), Richard G. Novak (pro hac vice, Pasadena CA), Michael N. Burt (pro hac vice, San Francisco CA), Staci Visser (Brown, Bradshaw & Moffat, SLC); Judge: Hon. Tony F. Graf, Jr.; Case No. 251403576, Fourth Judicial District, Provo. Materiality: omitting it misattributes the filing and loses the two out-of-state capital-defence specialists and the judge's name.

- **M-03** (Intro, p. 1): Brief asserts the State charged Robinson on September 16, 2025 with capital aggravated murder "and other lesser offenses," had "over ten months to investigate," and presented its aggravator evidence at the preliminary hearing "in July 2026." Materiality: the ten-month framing is the brief's lead rhetorical move; also its date-of-charging and hearing-date claims.
- **M-04** (Intro, p. 1): KGRD, Utah Code § 76-5-202(2)(a)(iii), is described as "the sole aggravator alleged in the Information," which "in theory exposes Mr. Robinson to the potential punishment of death." Materiality: the entire architecture rests on there being one death-eligibility aggravator; footnote 1 (p. 3) adopts the "KGRD" shorthand.
- **M-05** (Intro, p. 1): Preemptive record-locking: the State's failure "cannot in any manner be attributed to any orders by this Court limiting its presentation"; no evidence or expert excluded, no time limit; and — notably — the aggravator presentation "was not based upon hearsay evidence," so Rule 1102(c)(1) does not apply. Materiality: forestalls any State cure/reopening; also creates an internal tension with the global hearsay argument (M-06) that a summary must record, not resolve.

## B. Legal arguments and relief

- **M-06** (unnumbered threshold argument, p. 2): The State's "extensive use of hearsay deemed reliable by" Rule 1102 violates U.S. Const. amends. VI, VIII, XIV, Utah Const. art. I § 1, and separation of powers; preserved via prior briefing (Docs. 525, 570, 631, 678) and a continuing objection at the hearing. Relief: "This Court must decline bind over on all charges." Materiality: this is the ONLY argument reaching Counts 1–5; omit it and the summary wrongly says the defence attacked only the aggravator/enhancements.
- **M-07** (p. 2) [defence's second-hand description of the State's case]: Identity evidence for all counts (StBr:9-10) is characterised as Robinson–Twiggs communications, Discord communications, and a UVU-surveillance identification (StEx 16.1, 16.2), all coming from or made "presumptively admissible through" a recorded Utah County Attorney's Office interview of Lance Twiggs (StEx 16). Materiality: pins the whole identity case to one hearsay source, per the defence.
- **M-08** (p. 2): The Court "would not allow Mr. Robinson to seek to subpoena" Twiggs from another state to testify (Doc. 625). Materiality: the confrontation grievance underlying M-06; also a docket fact.
- **M-09** (Argument I heading, pp. 2–3): KGRD unsupported "as a Matter of Law" given "the Single Shot From a High-Powered, Scoped Rifle From a Rooftop Vantage That Hit the Intended Target." Relief: strike the aggravator. Materiality: the heading itself embeds the defence's factual theory of the shot.
- **M-10** (I.a, pp. 3–5): Constitutional-narrowing argument: Eighth/Fourteenth Amendments require narrow construction of aggravators (Gregg, Proffitt, Lewis v. Jeffers, State v. Wood (Utah)); Gregg/Proffitt upheld KGRD only because state high courts construed it narrowly (Chenault vs. Jarrell contrast; Alvord; Lucas fn. 2).
- **M-11** (I.b, pp. 5–10): Utah trilogy — Pierre (1977), Johnson (1987), Sosa-Hurtado II (2019) — read by the defence to require, "as a factual matter," that the defendant "actually discharges multiple rounds, hitting and/or killing" others in a "concatenating series of events." Materiality: this synthesis is the defence's gloss on the case law, the legal core of the brief; a summary must attribute it as the defence's reading, not as the holding.
- **M-12** (I.b, pp. 8–9): The governing test as the brief states it: Sosa-Hurtado I's three factors (temporal relationship; spatial proximity; actual threat, direct or via stray/ricochet), endorsed in Sosa-Hurtado II, plus Price/Johnson "zone of danger" language — "likelihood or high probability of great risk of death… not just a mere possibility," known to the defendant. Materiality: the yardstick every factual claim is measured against.
- **M-13** (I.c preliminary, pp. 10–11): Accusation that the State "makes little effort to distinguish between the evidence it presented and inferences"; speculation-vs-inference framework from Murphy, 2026 UT App 38, ¶ 10 (quoting Prisbrey, Carrera); no inference-stacking (Cristobal). Materiality: the brief's method — it purports to give an inference-free record recitation (items M-40 to M-50).
- **M-14** (I.d intro, pp. 15–16): The State's two KGRD theories [second-hand]: (1) "line of sight"/"line of fire," (2) "everyone near"/"anyone near"; both said to violate U.S. Const. amend. VIII/XIV and Utah Const. art. I § 9 if adopted. Includes the arguendo reservation "[e]ven assuming that one can infer a knowledge of some risk to the shooter."
- **M-15** (I.d.i, pp. 16–17): Factual rebuttal of line-of-fire as to the "questioner": single bullet travelled east-to-west "at a downward slope" from above; Kirk elevated on a platform; "the only evidence presented supports that the bullet travelled above, not through, the crowd." Materiality: the brief's central ballistic-geometry claim, made in its own voice.
- **M-16** (I.d.i, pp. 17–19): Legal rebuttal distinguishing Watson, Silvia, Reid, Buck, Wood (Ariz.): each involved "conduct directed at the endangered person"; "Utah has never adopted" KGRD for a single shot that hit only the intended target "merely because other people were in the vicinity." Materiality: the brief's dispositive legal proposition for theory 1.
- **M-17** (I.d.ii.1, pp. 20–23) [second-hand]: The five State "knowledge" inferences enumerated a)–e): (a) shooter observed security personnel; (b) knew of people behind the tent; (c) four cartridges in the rifle; (d) practice targets in the apartment; (e) rifle taken apart/reassembled (StBr:11). Materiality: the summary must capture all five — the rebuttal structure is point-by-point.
- **M-18** (rebuttal (a), pp. 20–21): 35–44-second prone window; Agent Hull "can't answer" what the shooter saw (PH2:68); "the only reasonable inference… was that the shooter observed Mr. Kirk through his scope."
- **M-19** (rebuttal (b), p. 21): StEx 9 shows "no one directly behind" the tent centre (PH2:70); one cannot see through the tent (PH2:84-85); the 8:30 AM amphitheater visit, "three and a half hours before the event," cannot show knowledge of the later crowd layout.
- **M-20** (rebuttal (c), pp. 21–22): A loaded rifle is "just as likely" mere capability as expectation of missing (Cristobal equal-inference rule); "the shooter did not miss his intended target and did not chamber another round," spent case left chambered (PH4:106, 130-31). Materiality: contains a striking defence-voice factual assertion (shooter accuracy).
- **M-21** (rebuttal (d), p. 22): No evidence of when the targets were used, with what weapon, under what conditions, or that Robinson fired all the shots.
- **M-22** (rebuttal (e), pp. 22–23): No evidence the rifle "was in pieces at any time"; gait "impaired by something long in his pant leg — the reasonable inference… a fully assembled rifle"; the screwdriver (PH1:72-73, fn. 12: "a red and black screwdriver… 10 or 15 feet in from the… guardrail") proves neither disassembly nor accuracy loss (Gallegos). Includes arguendo reservation "[e]ven if the Court draws the inference" of a rifle–screwdriver connection.
- **M-23** (I.d.ii.2, pp. 23–24): "Even assuming arguendo that the shooter had knowledge that there were other individuals near Mr. Kirk," presence alone is legally insufficient; distinguishes Pa. cases Rios, Ly, Smith, Wright (enclosed rooms, someone "directly next to" victim, multiple shots, ricochets); contrast list in the brief's voice: open-air arena, no one directly next to Kirk, no one under the tent on the struck side or "behind him in the breezeway," single shot, no ricochets. Materiality: the arguendo concession plus the brief's canonical fact-contrast.
- **M-24** (I.e, pp. 24–27): Comparative survey ("A Plenary of Jurisdictions"): Oklahoma (Lockett, Valdez, Littlejohn, Brecheen), Wyoming (Engberg, Olsen), Alabama (White), federal 18 U.S.C. § 3592(c)(5) (McVeigh, Bin Laden), plus fn. 13 string cite (Johnson (Mo.), Hazelton, Carver, Johnson (Tenn.), Porter, Sandoval). Littlejohn is quoted as the on-point single-shot analog: "Only one shot was fired. This shot hit its intended victim." Materiality: Littlejohn is the brief's best factual analog; dropping the survey loses the comparative spine.
- **M-25** (Argument II, pp. 27–29): Count Six (witness tampering, Utah Code § 76-8-508) must be stricken: telling Twiggs to "ask for a lawyer and stay silent" was Fifth-Amendment-consistent, "purely altruistic" advice under United States v. Peterson ("the inverse is therefore true"); quotes Information at 3 ("directing his roommate to stay silent"). Materiality: the whole count-specific defence and its single controlling authority.
- **M-26** (II, p. 28): The full advice text quoted from StEx 16.1: "If any police ask you questions, ask for a lawyer and stay silent. My lawyer should be Doug Terry… make sure the police follow the right procedures, proper warrants and stuff, but be polite and respectful of course." Materiality: verbatim text of the conduct charged in Count Six, per the defence's exhibit reading.
- **M-27** (II, p. 28): Extended context quotations from the Robinson–Twiggs exchange (StEx 16.1), quoted by the defence itself: "Im gonna turn myself in willingly, one of my neighbors here is a deputy for the sheriff"; parents willing to help; "leave the room alone. The feds will search it top to bottom"; "I highly doubt it" (re avoiding prison); "You are all I worry about love"; "Don't talk to any media please"; "I will write to you as often as possible." Materiality: the brief's own selection of message evidence — a summary that omits these misses both the record content and the "context shows altruism" methodology.
- **M-28** (Argument III, pp. 29–30): Count Seven (Utah Code § 76-3-203-10(2), violent offense in presence of child under 14) must be stricken: State's video shows "two children, in fact, present" (StEx 6), but no evidence the shooter knew — ~400 feet, 35–44 seconds; morning campus walk insufficient; "[n]one of the footage shows [him] passing by or near individuals that are clearly minors"; college campus contrasted with an "obviously occupied elementary school." Materiality: contains an express factual concession (children present) with knowledge alone contested.
- **M-29** (III.a, p. 30): The identical "presence of a child" aggravating factor (Utah Code § 76-3-203.9) alleged "in connection with Counts One and Two" must be stricken for the same reason. Materiality: reveals a charging-structure fact (which counts carry this factor) a summary would otherwise lack.
- **M-30** (III.b, pp. 30–31): [second-hand] The State's "backup position" — that sentencing enhancements are not subject to proof at a preliminary hearing — rebutted via Apprendi: any fact increasing punishment (except criminal history) is an element; probable-cause right "extends to enhancements." Both § 76-3-203.9 and the victim-targeting enhancement (§ "6-3-203.14" as printed) said to be subject to Apprendi. Materiality: a distinct legal-scope dispute; also the brief's Apprendi citation prints "(1980)" while its text says "in the year 2000" (see M-58).
- **M-31** (Argument IV, pp. 31–33): Victim targeting enhancement (Utah Code § 76-3-203(14); attribute "political expression," § 76-3-203(14)(1)(k)) lacks reliable evidence: the Englehardt Rule 1102 statement (Exhibit 5.1) identifies no specific pre-2025-09-10 Kirk statements nor any known to/motivating Robinson; the only other fact is "I had enough of his hatred" (StEx 16.1) — "[h]e refers to 'hatred' and nothing more"; per Twiggs, no prior Robinson–Twiggs communication about Kirk. Relief: "The victim targeting enhancement must be stricken."
- **M-32** (IV, pp. 32–33): The filing contains a passage characterising the State's motive theory as resting on Robinson's sexuality and the roommate's gender identity [the filing's second-hand description of the State; involves a private individual — noted here only for existence and argumentative role]; the filing labels this "the State's speculation" and not "an evidentiary substitute" for proof of targeting. Materiality: without noting this section's existence and role, the summary misses how the brief says the State bridges its motive gap.
- **M-33** (IV, p. 33): In its own voice the brief asserts Kirk "was, in fact, widely viewed as expressing hatred and intolerance" on the two topics the State raised. Materiality: a rare brief-voice characterisation of the victim's public reputation; blending it into the State's position would misattribute it.
- **M-34** (IV, p. 33): Investigative-scope null claim in the brief's voice: after searches of "his residence, his parents' residence, his computers, his telephone, Mr. Twiggs' telephone, and hundreds of law enforcement interviews," nothing supports the enhancement "other than that single criticism of Mr. Kirk's 'hatred'." Materiality: an absence-of-evidence claim with a stated (defence-asserted) search scope.
- **M-35** (Conclusion, p. 33): Relief stack, near-verbatim: hearsay reliance means "[f]or this reason alone, this Court must decline bindover"; insufficient evidence "as a matter of law, to satisfy the sole alleged aggravator"; and "the Court should decline to bindover on the State's alleged aggravators and Counts 6 and 7." Materiality: the operative ask; note the conclusion asks to strike the aggravator AND decline bindover globally — both layers must appear.

## C. Exhibit and docket designators (complete lists)

- **M-36**: State's Exhibits cited: StEx 1; 3; 3.2; 4; 5; 5.1 (Englehardt Rule 1102 witness statement); 6 (witness "AW" video, 22 seconds); 7; 8; 9; 10.3; 11 (medical examiner's report, unpublished); 12.1; 12.4 (UVU surveillance compilations; 12.1 = zoomed 12.4, fn. 6); 16 (recorded Twiggs interview); 16.1; 16.2; 16.3; 19–22 (cartridges); 25 (shooting targets); 32 (rifle). Materiality: the complete exhibit map a summary needs; no other exhibits are cited.
- **M-37**: Docket documents cited: Docs. 525, 570, 631, 678 (prior hearsay/1102 briefing); Doc. 625 (Twiggs subpoena ruling); the Information (quoted at "Information at 3"); the State's brief "StBr" with pin cites 2-3, 9-10, 11, 12, 14, 16, 16-17. Materiality: acquisition targets and the existence of a State brief this filing answers.
- **M-38**: Transcript citations span four hearing days — PH1, PH2, PH3 (residence search, PH3:35), PH4 — with one cite-form anomaly: day-2 cites appear as both "PH2:…" and "TR2:33-35"/"TR2:34-35." Materiality: confirms ≥4 transcript volumes are cited; the TR2/PH2 switch matters when cross-referencing the banked transcripts.
- **M-39**: Witness/person roster as cited: Officer Bagley (PH1), Agent Hull (PH2), Agent Jennifer Faumuina (PH4, forensic investigator), "Mr. Sturgill" (State counsel, quoted at PH1:204), Pastor David Englehardt (Ex 5.1 declarant), Lance Twiggs (StEx 16 interview), witness "AW" (initials only, StEx 6); "Doug Terry" appears only inside the quoted text message as Robinson's lawyer. Materiality: maps hearing days to witnesses; a summary without it can't trace PH cites.

S.B. 1314 (2019); Utah R. Crim. P. 7B(b); Utah R. Evid. 1102; Utah R. Jud. Admin. 4-202.02(4)(N); U.S. Const. amends. V, VI, VIII, XIV; Utah Const. art. I §§ 1, 9. - **M-42**: Delegitimising footnotes on the State's authorities: Arizona repealed its KGRD aggravator in 2019 and made its absence mitigating (fn. 3); New Jersey abolished the death penalty in 2007 (fn. 4); Pennsylvania has had a death-penalty moratorium "[f]or over a decade" (fn. 10). Materiality: the brief argues the State's key out-of-state authority comes from jurisdictions that abandoned the aggravator or the penalty.

## E. Additional characterisations of the State's brief/conduct (all second-hand descriptions by the defence)

- **M-43** (fn. 5, p. 11): Accusation that the State "quoted liberally" from the unpublished medical examiner's report (StEx 11) in a public filing (StBr:2-3), contrary to Utah R. Jud. Admin. 4-202.02(4)(N) — "another example of the State publicizing private information"; quotes Sturgill's courtroom non-publication request (PH1:204). Materiality: a distinct misconduct-flavoured accusation, plus the record fact that StEx 11 was never published.
- **M-44** (fn. 8, p. 13): State's claim that "[a]t least two individuals were standing under the tent" (StBr:16) called "contrary to the evidence" and "indicative of the State's reckless recitation of the evidence in its brief." Materiality: an express factual-accuracy attack on the opposing brief.
- **M-45** (fn. 11, p. 17): State's "a few feet" questioner-to-Kirk distance (StBr:12): "there was no evidence of the distance submitted to the Court."
- **M-46** (fn. 9, p. 14): "The State did not show footage of [Robinson's] movements in and around campus during the hearing, only the footage from the parking structures." Materiality: gap between what was played and what the State's brief describes.
- **M-47** (p. 19, StBr:14, 16-17): The State's "everyone near" formulation quoted as: the shooter "created a great risk of death to everyone near Mr. Kirk," and "a zone of danger encompasses everyone near a shooting victim" (relying on Pennsylvania cases). Materiality: the actual wording of the theory the brief spends Part d.ii defeating.

## F. Factual assertions in the brief's own voice about 2025-09-10 / the investigation

(All framed by the brief as a recitation of preliminary-hearing evidence; each remains a party's claim.)

- **M-48** (p. 11): "several thousand" people at the UVU amphitheater (PH1:65, 68; StEx 1); Kirk struck 12:23:28 PM by a projectile "on the left side of his neck," fatal (StEx 11; PH1:67); "The best evidence of the events… are the videos." Materiality: time-of-shot to the second and the brief's evidentiary hierarchy claim.
- **M-49** (pp. 12–13): Rooftop timeline from StEx 12.1/12.4: walkway view from 12:15:20; shooter over the "couple feet high" guardrail (12.4 at 06:18; PH1:46-47); 12:22:12 running west across Losee roof; 12:22:25 drops and crawls southwest; reaches edge ~12:22:44 (movement to ~12:22:56); prone 15–30 seconds (Hull, PH2:67); 12:23:28 rises, runs northeast, drops off the roof; shoe print in grass (PH1:98-99). Defence computes "in position… for approximately 35-44 seconds." Materiality: the 35–44-second figure is a defence computation reused throughout Arguments I and III — a summary must mark its provenance.
- **M-50** (pp. 12, 16): Bagley: "a clear line of sight between the tent and the top of the Losee Center" (PH1:53-54, 117; StExs 3.2, 4); Losee "directly east of amphitheater" (PH1:27); Losee has 4–5 levels (fn. 7, PH1:52). Materiality: the defence itself banks the "clear line of sight" quote and later re-deploys it against the enclosed-space cases.
- **M-51** (pp. 12–13): Video-geometry readings: StEx 7 — questioner separated from Kirk by barrier, grass patch "of unknown dimensions," table; Kirk seated on an elevated platform; exactly one individual under the tent, to Kirk's right/behind, "on the opposite side of where the bullet struck"; no timestamps. StEx 8 — two apparent security personnel in front/diagonal in the grass; overhead camera angle; shot at 00:48; guard enters frame 3 seconds after. StEx 9 (from 12:21:14) — no one immediately behind the "American Comeback" tent centre at the shot (PH2:69); tent not see-through (PH2:84-85). StEx 6 — 22 seconds from witness AW's perspective, no timestamp. Materiality: these frame-by-frame readings are the brief's entire factual case on theories 1 and 2.
- **M-52** (pp. 13–14): Faumuina measurements: slope distance rooftop-to-tent "approximately 415 feet"; elevation difference "approximately 68 feet"; straight-line 410 feet (PH4:91-92). Materiality: the only distance figures in the brief; feed the ~400-ft claim in Argument III.
- **M-53** (p. 14): Rifle: Mauser model 98, .30-06 caliber, scoped, bolt-action, recovered in a wooded area across the street from the Losee NE corner (PH2:126; PH4:96-97; StExs 10.3, 32); on bolt manipulation, one "fired cartridge case" still in the chamber plus three unfired cartridges (PH2:102; StExs 19-22); case fired from the recovered weapon (PH4:130-31). Materiality: the single-shot/no-rechamber fact pattern is the fulcrum of the whole KGRD argument.
- **M-54** (pp. 14–15): Campus-movements timeline (attributed to "individual[s] State's witnesses identified as Mr. Robinson"): four parking-structure entries/exits on 2025-09-10 (PH1:212-13) — ~8:30 AM entry, amphitheater visit, spoke with "some representatives from TPUSA," back to vehicle ~9:25 AM (PH2:29-30); ~10:00 AM entry, Chick-fil-A in Sorenson Center, wooded area across Campus Drive, appears at the walkway railing by the Losee roof, left "just prior to 11:00am" (PH2:31-32); returns 11:53:05 AM "in different clothing" walking with "[a] limp" (StEx 12.4 at 03:25); on the walkway ~12:15 PM; after the shooting "a vehicle is seen matching Mr. Robinson's." Materiality: the day's full movement chronology, including the defence's careful "identified as" attribution formula — flattening that formula into "Robinson did X" would misstate the brief.
- **M-55** (p. 15): Residence search: St. George apartment shared with Twiggs (PH3:35); "shooting targets [with] perforations" consistent with bullet holes in a first-floor closet (PH4:113-16; StEx 25); pattern of perforations progressively closer to centre. Materiality: the physical evidence behind State knowledge-inference (d).
- **M-56** (p. 15): Brief's own statement: the admitted Robinson–Twiggs communications "indicate Mr. Robinson's intention to kill Charlie Kirk," quoting StEx 16.3: "I had the opportunity to take out Charlie Kirk and I took it," with "no mention of any threat or intended harm to any other individual(s)." Materiality: the filing's most striking near-concession — it accepts intent-to-kill-Kirk as the record's import while contesting only risk-to-others; a summary omitting this materially misstates the defence posture.

## G. Concessions, non-concessions, reservations

- **M-57** (whole brief): The merits arguments (I–IV) never contest that Robinson was the shooter; they operate within the State's evidence, and the brief itself asserts "the shooter did not miss his intended target," "the only reasonable inference… the shooter observed Mr. Kirk through his scope," and that the pant-leg object was reasonably "a fully assembled rifle." Identity is contested solely through the hearsay-reliability/decline-bindover-on-all-charges argument (M-06/M-07); there is no merits argument against Counts 1–5, and no count-by-count list of the "other lesser offenses" appears anywhere in the brief. Explicit arguendo reservations at pp. 16, 22, 23 (see M-14, M-22, M-23); express concession that two children were "in fact, present" (M-28); express concession the court imposed no evidentiary or time limits (M-05). Materiality: this is the single easiest thing for a summary to get wrong — either "the defence conceded identity" or "the defence contested identity" would each be false without this layered description.

## H. Internal anomalies (raw data for citation verification)

- **M-58** (various pages): Errors/oddities inside the brief that a summary must record rather than silently correct: Apprendi printed "530 U.S. 466 (1980)" (TOA p. iii and p. 30) while the text says the holding came "in the year 2000"; "its 1997 decision in State v. Pierre" (p. 5 — Pierre is dated 1977 elsewhere in the same brief); heading "A Plenary of Jurisdictions" (p. 24); "each element of each of the charged evidence" (twice, pp. 2 and 33); "Utah Code § 6-3-203.14" (p. 31, apparently missing "76-"); hyphenated "§ 76-3-203-10(2)"; Wood (Ariz.), 881 P.2d 1158, pin-cited "Id. at 69" (pp. 18–19, inconsistent with that reporter's pagination); "the defendant filed multiple shots" (p. 8); "personas other than the decedent" (p. 19); TR2 vs PH2 cite-form switch (M-38). Materiality: any Tier 1 verification pass will hit these; unrecorded, they read as transcription errors in OUR extraction rather than defects in the filing itself.

End of inventory. 58 items, M-01 through M-58. No files were created or edited.
